transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-05-15 16:00 UTC
Duration: 68 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Mateo Alvarez (Redwood SRE); Elena Park (Aurelia Head of ML), Marcus Li (Aurelia Platform Eng), Samantha Ortiz (Aurelia Security Arch), Ravi Desai (Ops)

Summary (auto): quick alignment on hemispheric routing idea, KV cache warmup plan, and on-prem SLA items. Agreed to run benchmarks and share configs.

[00:00] Jordan: ok welcome everyone, thanks for carving out the time. we wanted to focus on the routing/failover architecture and the k v cache warmup implications for the hemispheric setup.
[00:17] Elena: thanks jordan. we've been getting more traffic from eu and apac simultaneously and our p99s spike when we cold start new regional pools. want to avoid double-provisioning.
[00:31] Marcus: real quick, our constraints: max budget cap for inference is 40k month right now, also we need on-prem for the eu-privacy zone for some regulated customers.
[00:45] Jordan: got it. priya, do you want to kick into the policy design?
[00:48] Priya: yeah sure. so the hemispheric routing idea is basically two regions per hemisphere — primary+failover per hemisphere — route by latency first, then capacity, then cost. we suggested a weighted policy: latency threshold 120ms, if exceeded route to sibling region; if sibling at 85% capacity and still bad, fall back to cold-host in a lower-cost region.
[01:12] Marcus: when you say 120ms is that backend or network? what's included?
[01:18] Priya: it's observed p50+p90 for our runtime path — includes edge hop + runtime queuing but excludes client-side. rough number for us for that model family with batch size 4 and kv warm is around that.
[01:33] Elena: side question — how does k v cache get moved or warmed when you route between hemispheres? i.e. we can't have perfect cache across oceans.
[01:43] Priya: correct. we propose sticky routing for short lived sessions so the kv stays local, but for stateless request patterns we do async k v prewarm: when we detect traffic shift we proactively fetch likely prefixes to the target pool. that's the 'prefetch + soft-evict' pattern.
[02:02] Marcus: prefetch sounds heavy, how do you avoid overfetch and cost?
[02:06] Priya: we use a scoring function — frequency * recency / token-cost — only top N prefixes, N adaptive to bandwidth. and we throttle prefetch during peak.
[02:19] Samantha: for on-prem we need to know where the KMS calls happen — we cannot have key material cross regions. does prefetch require decrypting cache objects?
[02:29] Priya: no, cache entries are opaque blobs. the prefetch copies encrypted blobs; decryption happens only in the target region's HSM/KMS. you'll need the same keyspace or a federated KMS trust if you want seamless access.
[02:45] Samantha: federated trust is tough for us. we prefer local keys. can the system support per-region keys?
[02:52] Jordan: yes, Redwood Private supports per-cluster KMS integration; we recommend mirrored but independent keys and a handshake to validate replication fingerprints. we'll put the architecture note in the security pack.
[03:05] Ravi: ok that helps. back to runtime — what about batching? we see good throughput gains but p99 gets worse if we batch too aggressively.
[03:15] Priya: right — continuous batching helps amortize cost but increases tail. our suggestion: latency-sensitive routes use small micro-batches (1-4 tokens), while cost-sensitive routes enable larger batching with a hard p99 cap. the routing policy can mark routes as "latency-first" or "cost-first".
[03:34] Marcus: can we have the same model quantized in on-prem but full precision in hosted? are there quality regressions we should expect?
[03:41] Priya: yes quantization profiles differ. 8-bit dynamic often has minor hallucination increase for longer-context prompts. we recommend running a small eval set during pilot to measure WER/QA diffs. also quantized models load faster — helps cold-start.
[03:58] Elena: about cold-start — we observe 2x latency for model load plus cache warm. what's your mitigation?
[04:05] Mateo: two levels: 1) keep a tiny warm pool with minimal replicas ready for quick start, 2) KV warmup: proactive prefix caching based on traffic patterns. the tiny warm pool costs a bit more but reduces p99 significantly.
[04:21] Marcus: what's the eviction strategy if we have memory pressure in the on-prem GPU hosts?
[04:26] Priya: LRU with frequency boosting for prefixes tagged by recent production prompts. plus a grace eviction window where we serialize evicted prefixes to encrypted object store for faster rehydrate. note the serialization step still pays I/O cost.
[04:42] Elena: how about cross-region DR? say eu primary goes down — what's the expected failover time?
[04:48] Jordan: policy can be immediate (route switch in <30s) for simple DNS/edge changes but KV recovery to steady-state depends on warmup. with warmup prefetch it's 2-6 minutes to reach 90% of baseline; without it's longer.
[05:05] Samantha: that's a big delta for regulated SLAs. do you have metrics we can use in an SLO?
[05:10] Mateo: yes we have benchmarks. we'll share a 48h run showing p50/p95/p99 profiles with different warmup strategies. we'll annotate with sequences lengths and batch sizes.
[05:20] Elena: please include a scenario where apac spikes 3x and eu is 0 — we want to ensure hemispheric doesn't overprovision.
[05:27] Jordan: good call. we'll include a simulation.
[05:30] Marcus: curious — if you route to sibling region, token cost sometimes rises. any cost-metering per route?
[05:37] Priya: yes console-level cost attribution by route and model variant. you can set cost thresholds to disable expensive fallbacks and instead prefer degraded latency routes.
[05:46] Marcus: and do you support sticky session affinity for clients behind LB?
[05:50] Priya: yes cookie-based or token-based affinity; we also support request hashing for longer term affinities.
[05:58] Elena: switching gears — on-prem deployment mechanics: what's the control-plane talkback? we need to keep customer control plane on-prem or VPC-hosted.
[06:08] Jordan: for Redwood Private we run a management plane connector that can be deployed in VPC; control plane communications are TLS mutual auth, telemetry stripped per your retention policies. you can also opt for full air-gapped install and get a local UI.
[06:23] Samantha: audit logs — retention and tamper evidence?
[06:27] Mateo: logs are shipped to your SIEM endpoint. we sign logs with a rotation key and provide verifiable checksums. retention on-prem is configurable. we'll include the spec.
[06:39] Marcus: what about orchestrating failover with our existing infra — we use an internal traffic controller. can we plug the Redwood routing decisions into it?
[06:48] Priya: yes, we expose a small decision endpoint and a webhook. you can also pull our route table via API and implement your own controller.
[06:56] Elena: can we see a demo of the policy editor?
[06:59] Jordan: sure — we'll schedule a short demo next week.
[07:03] <20 minutes jump — deep technical exchange removed for brevity>
[27:05] Priya: we did want to call out quantization cold-start nuance: some kernels need JIT compile at first request, which can add 200-400ms in some hardware setups. on-prem tends to see higher JIT cost if statically linked libs differ.
[27:22] Marcus: oh that's important for our on-prem clusters with older GPUs. can you bypass JIT with warmed kernels?
[27:28] Mateo: yes — pre-compile kernels during image bake or at first deployment; we include a kernel cache artifact that can be distributed to nodes. that reduces first-run jitter.
[27:38] Samantha: any security concerns distributing kernel cache? it could leak model signatures?
[27:43] Priya: kernel caches are generic binary blobs, not model-specific weights. still we sign them and verify integrity at load time.
[27:52] Elena: what's the recommended pilot shape — dedicated small pool in eu, mirrored warm pool in apac, and hosted fallback in na?
[27:59] Jordan: that fits. pilot suggestion: 3x small GPUs eu primary (warm pool 2), apac 2x small GPUs warm, na hosted fallback autoscale. measurement targets: p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, cost per 1000 tokens.
[28:18] Marcus: ok let's talk DR playbook specifics — do you have a runbook template?
[28:23] Priya: yes we have a DR runbook with steps: detect, divert, prewarm, validate, and rollback. detect uses health probes + synthetic transactions. divert is policy flip with nasal care — sorry — with canary traffic first, then full. prewarm runs prefetchers and spins up the warm pool.
[28:44] Elena: walk me through validation after failover — how do we ensure quality parity?
[28:49] Mateo: run sample eval prompts and check output hash/signature and a small prompt-level QA. we also have loss-of-cache indicators that show likely divergence.
[28:59] Samantha: in our compliance world we need auditable timestamps of failover and who initiated it. does your console provide that?
[29:05] Jordan: yes every policy change and failover event is logged with actor and immutable IDs; we can export to your audit system.
[29:14] Marcus: any quick wins to reduce p99 immediately without big infra change?
[29:18] Priya: yes: reduce default batch window, enable micro-batching for latency routes, increase minimum warm replicas from 0 to 1, and prewarm top 200 prefixes. small changes, big effect.
[29:31] Elena: sounds good. one more question on cost modeling for failover — how do we estimate double-run cost during failover?
[29:37] Jordan: our cost model projects warm replica minutes + prefetch egress; we'll give a spreadsheet with sensitivities for 10/30/100% spike scenarios.
[29:47] Samantha: for the on-prem SLA, we need guaranteed RTO for region failure — can Redwood commit to an RTO?
[29:54] Jordan: hosted/dedicated tiers we put in SLOs; for on-prem, it's trickier since we depend on your network. we can commit to a documented playbook and target numbers but hard SLA unless we run the dedicated pilot and agree contractually.
[30:10] Marcus: understood. what about fallback fidelity — do you support fallback to a smaller model to preserve latency?
[30:16] Priya: yes model variant fallback is built-in: you can define a fallback chain (fp16 -> 8-bit quant -> distilled) and policies control when to drop to cheaper model. quality and cost deltas are visible in the console.
[30:29] Elena: what about data residency for logs and telemetry when using hybrid?
[30:33] Mateo: telemetry can be locally retained and only aggregated metrics sent to Redwood control plane; we can sign agreements for log residency.
[30:43] Jordan: ok let's go through the concrete deliverables — priya will produce the YAML and routing diagram; mateo will run the warmup benchmark; i'll compile pricing and pilot contract; samantha will get security checklist items.
[30:54] Elena: timeline? we want pilot in 6 weeks ideally.
[30:57] Jordan: doable if we get traffic patterns and infra access in one week.
[31:02] Marcus: one last nit — what happens to KV eviction when a node reappears after transient failure? do you rehydrate from peers or reconstruct?
[31:09] Priya: rehydrate from peer snapshots if available; otherwise rehydrate from object store; there is an asynchronous reconciliation pass that repairs missing prefixes.
[31:21] Elena: any final security note — encryption-in-transit and at-rest?
[31:25] Samantha: yes must be both, and HSM-backed key for model weights.
[31:29] Priya: agreed, that is supported.
[31:34] Jordan: ok wrapping — recap and next steps.
[31:38] <fast recap>
[31:40] Jordan: recap: we'll share routing policy + diagram, security pack, benchmark plan, and pricing. Aurelia provides traffic patterns + compliance list. target pilot start ~6 weeks.
[31:52] Elena: thanks everyone. we'll review the materials and sync.
[31:56] Jordan: thanks all. meeting adjourned.
